content: Oxford Review of Education, Vol. 20, No. 3, 1994 281 The Education of Children in Need: the impact of the Education Reform Act 1988, The Education Act 1993 and the Children Act 1989 RUTH SINCLAIR, ROGER GRIMSHAW & LOUISE GARNETT ABSTRACT This paper indicates some of the contradictory messages contained in the Children Act 1989, the Education and Reform Act 1988 and the Education Act 1993 in particular with regard to the role of the local authority and the rights of children. The concept of 'children in need' within the education system is examined and the key groups of young people who are 'children in need' are identified. Concerns about the education provision to 'children in need' are highlighted using the results of two recent research studies undertaken by the Bureau, Children in Residential EBD Schools and Adolescents Assessed by Social Services. The paper concludes with a postscript on more recent government policies for pupils with problems. INTRODUCTION Two cornerstones of British social policy-the responsibility of the state to ensure that all children are educated and that their welfare is safeguarded and promoted-have been subject in recent years to major changes in the legislative framework which underpins them. However, the thrust of this legislation in the form of the Children Act 1989 and the Education Reform Act 1988, together with the recently passed Education Act 1993, displays inconsistency: an inconsistency which is likely to mean that the needs within the education system of children, and particularly vulnerable children, will not be met. This paper starts by noting two key areas in which the legislation is contradictory; it then examines the concept of 'children in need' within the education system; finally, it uses the results from two recent research studies undertaken at the National Children's Bureau to highlight serious concerns about educational provision for children in need. CONTRADICTORY MESSAGES The thrust of the social policy agenda contained in the Children Act and the Education Acts is noticeably inconsistent in two key areas: the role of the local authority and the rights of children. Each will be discussed briefly. The role of the local authority The Children Act 1989 can be viewed as greatly enhancing the enabling powers of the This content downloaded from 91.229.248.152 on Tue, 17 Jun 2014 18:04:09 PM All use subject to JSTOR Terms and Conditions

282 Oxford Review of Education local authority to promote the welfare of all children 'in need', whereas the Education Reform Act 1988 has already reduced the role of the Local Education Author- ities (LEAs). The Children Act places a duty on the local authority 'to safeguard and promote the welfare of children within their area who are in need, by providing a range and level of services appropriate to meet those children's needs'. In contrast the Education Reform Act and the new provisions of the Education Act 1993 both aim, in a variety of ways, to limit the role of the Local Education Authority * through local management of schools (LMS), whereby most policy-making responsibilities have been transferred from the LEA to the governing bodies of individual schools; * local financial management, whereby LEAs are required to devolve at least 85% of their potential schools' budget to individual schools, with respon- sibility for financial decision-making, and therefore policy and resources, resting with boards of governors; and a corresponding inability of LEAs to maintain effective central services to assist schools in meeting particular needs; * the positive encouragement for schools to seek grant-maintained status and thereby opt out of the control of the local education authority; * 'open enrolment' policies which place schools in a competitive position and reduce the ability of the LEA to plan admissions and ensure appropriate schooling for all pupils. Children's rights Similar discrepancies can be seen in relation to children's rights. The Children Act contains specific statutory obligations which increase the rights of the child, most noticeably through consultation and participation in decision-making, the right to initiate action and the right to make representations or complaints. But within the education field, parents are seen as the customers as demonstrated by the introduction of a Parents' Charter as the mechanism for increasing the voice of the user in education: children have no rights to be heard. These inconsistencies in the legislation raise major questions about the power of local authorities to guarantee appropriate services to children in need within the education sector. If the functions and activities of the LEA, however imperfect they may be, are being removed, either by design or by consequence, then what mechanisms are going to replace these? How can Section 27 of the Children Act, which clearly identifies the responsibility of the provision of services to children in need as a corporate responsi- bility, be operated? In the absence of LEA oversight, how are individual schools developing policies and practices to meet the educational needs of children 'in need' and how is this being monitored? Who will act as the advocate for the 'unwanted' children in a market-led allocation system where individual schools will determine which pupils they wish to admit? These are all important questions which arise from the implementation of these key pieces of legislation, but which are not addressed by them. The Education of Children in Need 283 CHILDREN IN NEED A second set of issues arises when we ask-who are the children in need within the education system? The Children Act in s.17 (10) gives a clear definition of children in need. A child shall be taken to be in need if: (a) he is unlikely to achieve or maintain, or to have the opportunity of achieving or maintaining, a reasonable standard of health or development without the provision for him of services by a local authority under this Part; (b) his health or development is likely to be significantly impaired, or further impaired, without the provision for him of such service; or (c) he is disabled. This definition is further elaborated in s. 17 (11) of the Children Act where it states that development means 'physical, intellectual, emotional, social or behavioural develop- ment'. It would seem clear from this definition that anyone who is not receiving appro- priate educational provision is 'a child in need'. Here it is possible to identify four key groups of young people who are children in need within the education system: children with special educational needs; children who are 'looked after' by the local authority; children who are excluded from school; and persistent non-attenders at school. These four groups are not mutually exclusive, indeed, as the research we shall discuss later shows, failure to provide services at one level often means that children become 'looked after' or are placed in special residential schools. There is already evidence that each of these groups is likely to be adversely affected by the contra- dictions in the Children Act and the Education Acts. Only brief mention of that evidence will be provided in this paper as these are issues addressed elsewhere in this volume. Children with Special Educational Needs Under the 1981 Education Act 'a child has "special educational needs" if he has a learning difficulty which calls for special educational provision to be made for him' and, it continues, a child has a 'learning difficulty' if he fulfills the following criteria: (a) he has a significantly greater difficulty in learning than the majority of children of his age; or (b) he has a disability which either prevents or hinders him from making use of educational facilities of a kind generally provided in schools, within the area of the local authority concerned, for children of his age. The Warnock Committee estimated that 20% of pupils would have a special educa- tional need (SEN) during their school life, but as the special need of some pupils is temporary, the proportion of pupils with a special need at any one time was approxi- mately 16%. Currently 2.1% of the total school population of England and Wales have a state- ment and the majority of these children attend special schools-although research suggests that recent rises in these numbers have resulted from the recent legislative changes (Lunt & Evans, 1991). A report by the Audit Commission and HMI has been highly critical of the statementing process and welcome changes have since been included in the Education Act 1993 (Audit Commission and HMI, 1992). However, the other 18% of children with special needs but without 'statements' have received relatively little attention in either research or policy arenas. The problems of these children will be diverse and will include physical disabilities, learning difficulties, specific reading, writing or language problems, behavioural or social problems. However, unlike 'statemented' children, children in this group have very few, if any, formal mechanisms which enable them to be considered for additional resources which are allocated to meet individual needs. Additional resources may come in two ways-through the use of centrally maintained services, such as educational psychologists, or through an additional factor within the LEA formula for delegated budgets. However the component within the formula to meet additional/ social needs shows widespread variation in both method of derivation and amount (Lee, 1991). Experience suggests that formula funding has the effect of transferring funds from disadvantaged schools as the positive discrimination of the LEA is no longer possible, and within schools, of resources going to more 'academic' interests (Howsden, 1993). Children excluded from school The number of pupils being excluded from school is increasing (see for instance NUT, 1992; Islington, 1992). Even the woefully inadequate National Exclusions Reporting System, established by DFE, paints a picture of many pupils excluded from school and with alternatives which are usually limited and fall far short of giving these pupils access to a full curriculum (Audit Commission and HMI, 1992; DFE, 1992). The conse- quences for these pupils in terms of their subsequent life chances are particularly worrying (Blyth & Milner, 1993). These concerns have prompted some significant and welcome changes in the new education law. Only time will tell whether these will be sufficient to counteract other influences. Research into the schooling of children with emotional or behavioural difficulties suggests some of the reasons for increased exclusions among this group (Stirling, 1991). First, that exclusion is being used increasingly to relieve schools of problem pupils, as it has the advantage of being speedy and almost autonomous in comparison to the process of 'statementing' under the 1981 Education Act. Second, the exclusion of difficult pupils is likely to match the priorities of the headteacher and board of governors, who are aware of the need for the school to 'score well' on published performance measures if it is to retain or enhance its budget. Another worrying aspect centres on racial harassment and the disproportionate number of black pupils who are excluded; for example in Birmingham, African- Caribbean children make up 9% of the total school population but 30% of the children who are excluded (Mayet, 1992; see also Nottinghamshire CC, 1989). Children looked after by the Local Authority The third group who, by definition, are children in need are those children being looked after by the local authority. Research studies have consistently reported the very low level of educational attainment of children who are in contact with social services or in care (Jackson, 1989; Aldgate, 1990; Garnett, 1992). Other studies point to the problems of the education provided to children whilst in care (Hampshire SSD, 1991; Fletcher-Campbell & Hall, 1990). This concern was pointedly raised again in the Utting Report, Children in the Public Care, which recommends that joint subcommittees of Education and Social Services should include, within their remit, the development of strategies to meet the educa- tional needs of children in care (Utting, 1991). Such a recommendation once again raises questions about the viability of such corporate strategies, given the very reduced power of the LEA to influence the policies and practices of individual schools to ensure that the educational needs of all 'children in need' are met. Persistent non-school attenders Pupils fail to attend school regularly for a variety of reasons. The HMI suggest that these include 'for example, family circumstances, cultural and social expectations and economic pressures; apathy or even antipathy to school on the part of pupils or parents or both and the fact that some pupils, for whatever reason, prefer other ways of spending their time... Attendance is also substantially affected by what schools do. The curriculum, the liveliness and competence of the teaching, the quality of the relation- ships and of the school as a community'. In this latter context two significant factors are bullying and racial harassment (HMI, 1989). Non-school attendance is not a new phenomenon, nor is there evidence that it has risen markedly in recent years (Gray & Jesson, 1990). Each school is now required to collect and publish information on 'unauthorised absences', but the widespread vari- ation in the interpretation of this requirement suggests that the first set of published figures must be treated with extreme caution (DFE, 1993b). However, there is other evidence that indicates the level of school attendance is very variable between schools and appears to be associated as much with school management as with socio-economic factors (Carlen et al., 1992; Grimshaw & Pratt, 1986; DES, 1989). Whether non-attendance is viewed as a rational choice (the consumer reject- ing the service offered) or the result of individual, community or school pathologies, the outcome is often that the child or young person comes to the attention of the social services department or the juvenile justice system. In this sense, and because they are not receiving appropriate services, non-school attenders are children in need. Despite the obvious needs displayed by each of those groups of children, it was disappointing that in monitoring the first year of the Children Act, it appeared that social services departments are according these groups very low priority, unless they are being looked after or are included on the Child Protection Register. The definition of need in the Act is deliberately wide to reinforce the emphasis on preventive support and services to families ... A local authority cannot lawfully substitute any other definition. (Department of Health, 1991). So the definition of children in need still stands and is there to be used by those promoting the welfare of vulnerable children within the education sector. CHILDREN IN NEED WITHIN THE EDUCATION SYSTEM The critical necessity of finding new ways of ensuring that children in need within the education sector are given a higher priority is clearly demonstrated by two recent research studies undertaken by the National Children's Bureau. The first of these, undertaken by Roger Grimshaw, examined the provision of services to a group of young people resident in special schools for children with emotional and behavioural difficulties (EBD) (Grimshaw with Berridge, 1994). The second is a study of social work assessment of adolescents carried out in one London Borough by Louise Garett and Ruth Sinclair (Sinclair et al., 1993). The depressing findings from both these studies suggest that vulnerable children will increasingly fall through the education system as the role of the LEA is weakened and replaced by market forces. Children in Residential EBD Schools In this first study-children resident in EBD schools-67 children in four schools were included. Information was gathered on the referral process, the needs of the children, the services provided, the regimes in the schools and the outcomes for the children. This is a major study which covers a wide range of issues; for the purposes of this paper selected material is used to highlight the problems that will increasingly arise from the disjunction apparent between the legislative frameworks. First, some of the research findings. This research confirms that children resident in EBD schools are 'children in need' under the Children Act definition-the needs of the children were identified as family problems, difficulties with relationships, and non-compliance at home; school discipline and attainment; as well as disabilities and health difficulties. Indeed they displayed a continuum of need which is very similar to that of children being looked after by the local authority. Admission to a residential school is a major step for a child as most remain there for many years. Yet the process of referral, the criteria for referral, the professional help prior to referral are varied and show a lack of clarity. All of this is in marked contrast to the priority given by social services departments to 'gatekeep' care, and residential care in particular. For instance 16% had a specialist teacher, 12% had a special part-time class and 7% had a special full-time class for EBD. Nor were non-residential school services utilised prior to admission; only 13% had attended a day unit and only one child had attended a day special school for EBD pupils. This was despite the fact that many children had early contact with specialist services outside school, as shown in Table IV. It seems that specialist services were unable to help build effective programmes for difficult pupils in mainstream schools which had apparently exhausted their resources and patience (Moses et al., 1988; Hegarty, 1993). If this was so before LMS and the new competitive ethos between schools how will it be possible in the future? Will we see continuing expansion of referrals to special schools or will more of the children simply get less education? We have already been alerted to such a possibility by the Govern- ment's own advisors. If schools had a responsibility to 'buy in' psychological, welfare or medical services, such resource decisions would need to be balanced against other demands for scarce resources. This might encourage a tendency in schools to under-purchase such services...and there might be an unfortunate tendency for schools to be more reluctant to accept pupils who might need such services. (Coopers & Lybrand Deloitte, 1988) This study highlights the many similar issues that are faced by the residential EBD sector and the local authority care system-yet they are governed by different legis- lation. For instance, the residential EBD sector is now very comparable in size to that of local authority residential care, yet by comparison it has received little attention or scrutiny; the residents in both sectors are subject to high reported rates of abuse both before and during placement; each faces the challenge of control and physical restraint; of insufficiently trained care staff; and the crucially important task of maintaining contact with families. Yet this detailed look at practice in the EBD sector also shows there are major discrepancies between that and the principles and standards of child-care established by the Children Act. Here just a few examples are noted: * the inspection and regulation procedures have only been partially brought together-for instance the new Children Homes Regulations do not apply to this sector; * there is an absence of consultation with children-unlike the requirements of the Children Act to 'ascertain the wishes and feelings of children', this is not a requirement of education. Do these differences matter? In so far as the residential EBD sector is now a leading provider of residential care for children in need it is a matter of some concern that it is not subject to the same regulation and public scrutiny as those sectors governed by the Children Act. Adolescents assessed by Social Services We turn now to the second study which we are using to illustrate the importance of the concept of children in need within the education sector. The main purpose of this study was to examine the effectiveness of different forms of social work assessment with adolescents. Information was gathered on a group of 75 young people in one London borough, who were subject to assessment following one of three key events: consider- ation of care or accommodation, admission to care or accommodation, or a placement breakdown. Although the trigger events that called forth an assessment were related to social services provision, it was immediately clear from the assessment of these young people's needs that education was a hugely significant factor for young people. Indeed, both parents and social workers had identified 'persistent non-school attendance' as the main presenting problem for two-thirds of the sample who were of school age. Simply chronicling their educational status at the time of their assessment makes it abundantly clear why this should be the case. First of all, it is necessary to give some brief information about the sample of 75 young people. The focus of the study was on adolescents, so the modal age of the group was 15, with two-thirds of the sample aged between 14 and 16 years. A similar proportion (63%) were from minority ethnic groups, and from a very varied range of ethnic origins. Boys made up more than half of the group (55%) and tended to be younger than the girls. The vast majority (81%) were under school leaving age. Of these, their official educational status was that just over half (51%) were enrolled in mainstream schools; 13% were in special schools (day or boarding); 16% were receiving part-time education at home or in a special tuition unit (although hours were very varied and none more than half the time); 20% were not enrolled in any school or alternative provision. In addition, 28% of the group were subject to a statement of SEN or were going through the statementing process. Not only were one in five of this group not currently being provided with education, but for many this situation had prevailed for long periods of time. Indeed, in this sample one in four of all the school children had been out of school for more than one year at the time of their assessment. How could so many children fall through the education net? Three factors were at play. First, pupils waiting for a statement of SEN may not be offered any immediate alternative. This study included one young man who had been waiting two years for a statement of SEN and during that time he had not been provided with any form of education. Second, a high proportion of pupils permanently excluded from school had not been provided with any other form of educational support. Sixteen per cent of the research group had been excluded, three-quarters of them permanently. Third, even for those officially in school, many were very poor attenders. For both this group and those excluded this problem was often worse in their last year of school. In this situation social workers certainly believed that the edu- cation department was deliberately slow in responding to these young people's needs, or gave them such a low priority that they fell out of the system before being dealt with. The results of such a policy can be seen among the older school leavers in the sample group-fewer than a quarter had actually attended school up to their official leaving date-and none of them had any GCSEs or any other educational qualifications. This brief account of the educational background of this group of adolescents raises several issues: * the majority of these young people were not in care or being 'looked after' by the local authority, when this data was gathered. This highlights just why it is so crucially important to think about the education of children in need and not just about those within the care system; * the failure to identify or to deal adequately with school problems at an early stage increases the chances of these young people coming to the attention of the care or juvenile justice systems; * even when young people do become known to social services, the slowness of the educational assessment process can often lead to what may be called 'planning blight' in the social services. This is particularly so if there is a possibility that the education department will recommend a place in a special boarding school, which may have a major impact on social services care plans for the young person; * alternative education provision currently fails to meet the demand and in many cases is not of sufficient quality, as the government has acknowledged (Ofsted, 1993; DFE, 1993); * there is evidence of growing tension between professionals in education and SSDs, often despite feelings of goodwill and shared aims, but the ability to work together effectively is being hampered by arguments over budgets and the growing practice of having to contract or buy in services once freely exchanged. The irrefutable evidence of these two studies is of children in need within the education system: children who do not have 'the opportunity of achieving or maintaining a reasonably standard of development, or whose development is likely to be significantly impaired', because of a lack of services. All the evidence so far of the impact of the Education Reform Act 1988, now to be compounded by the Education Act 1993-in- creases in the numbers statemented and in children excluded from school, of new admissions policies, of the transfer of resources away from support services-makes it more urgent that an answer is found to the question: How are we to ensure that these children in need receive the range and level of services appropriate to their needs, as statutorily required by the Children Act 1989? The Education of Children in Need 291 POSTSCRIPT This article, written in 1993, was the basis of strong representations made by the National Children's Bureau to the government about the implications of the Education Act on 'children in need'. These representations helped to prompt responses from the DFE in the form of the circulars Pupils with Problems and The Code of Practice on Identification and Assessment of Special Educational Needs. In publishing this article in its original form we believe that it illustrates how research can help to influence the thinking of policy makers. It remains to be seen how far the above-mentioned circulars will be effective in counteracting the more adverse tenden- cies of the Education Act's provisions, to which this article refers. Oxford Review of Education, Vol. 20, No. 3, 1994 281 The Education of Children in Need: the impact of the Education Reform Act 1988, The Education Act 1993 and the Children Act 1989 RUTH SINCLAIR, ROGER GRIMSHAW & LOUISE GARNETT ABSTRACT This paper indicates some of the contradictory messages contained in the Children Act 1989, the Education and Reform Act 1988 and the Education Act 1993 in particular with regard to the role of the local authority and the rights of children. The concept of 'children in need' within the education system is examined and the key groups of young people who are 'children in need' are identified. Concerns about the education provision to 'children in need' are highlighted using the results of two recent research studies undertaken by the Bureau, Children in Residential EBD Schools and Adolescents Assessed by Social Services. The paper concludes with a postscript on more recent government policies for pupils with problems. INTRODUCTION Two cornerstones of British social policy-the responsibility of the state to ensure that all children are educated and that their welfare is safeguarded and promoted-have been subject in recent years to major changes in the legislative framework which underpins them. However, the thrust of this legislation in the form of the Children Act 1989 and the Education Reform Act 1988, together with the recently passed Education Act 1993, displays inconsistency: an inconsistency which is likely to mean that the needs within the education system of children, and particularly vulnerable children, will not be met. This paper starts by noting two key areas in which the legislation is contradictory; it then examines the concept of 'children in need' within the education system; finally, it uses the results from two recent research studies undertaken at the National Children's Bureau to highlight serious concerns about educational provision for children in need. CONTRADICTORY MESSAGES The thrust of the social policy agenda contained in the Children Act and the Education Acts is noticeably inconsistent in two key areas: the role of the local authority and the rights of children. Each will be discussed briefly. The role of the local authority The Children Act 1989 can be viewed as greatly enhancing the enabling powers of the This content downloaded from 91.229.248.152 on Tue, 17 Jun 2014 18:04:09 PM All use subject to JSTOR Terms and Conditions

282 Oxford Review of Education local authority to promote the welfare of all children 'in need', whereas the Education Reform Act 1988 has already reduced the role of the Local Education Author- ities (LEAs). The Children Act places a duty on the local authority 'to safeguard and promote the welfare of children within their area who are in need, by providing a range and level of services appropriate to meet those children's needs'. In contrast the Education Reform Act and the new provisions of the Education Act 1993 both aim, in a variety of ways, to limit the role of the Local Education Authority * through local management of schools (LMS), whereby most policy-making responsibilities have been transferred from the LEA to the governing bodies of individual schools; * local financial management, whereby LEAs are required to devolve at least 85% of their potential schools' budget to individual schools, with respon- sibility for financial decision-making, and therefore policy and resources, resting with boards of governors; and a corresponding inability of LEAs to maintain effective central services to assist schools in meeting particular needs; * the positive encouragement for schools to seek grant-maintained status and thereby opt out of the control of the local education authority; * 'open enrolment' policies which place schools in a competitive position and reduce the ability of the LEA to plan admissions and ensure appropriate schooling for all pupils. Children's rights Similar discrepancies can be seen in relation to children's rights. The Children Act contains specific statutory obligations which increase the rights of the child, most noticeably through consultation and participation in decision-making, the right to initiate action and the right to make representations or complaints. But within the education field, parents are seen as the customers as demonstrated by the introduction of a Parents' Charter as the mechanism for increasing the voice of the user in education: children have no rights to be heard. These inconsistencies in the legislation raise major questions about the power of local authorities to guarantee appropriate services to children in need within the education sector. If the functions and activities of the LEA, however imperfect they may be, are being removed, either by design or by consequence, then what mechanisms are going to replace these? How can Section 27 of the Children Act, which clearly identifies the responsibility of the provision of services to children in need as a corporate responsi- bility, be operated? In the absence of LEA oversight, how are individual schools developing policies and practices to meet the educational needs of children 'in need' and how is this being monitored? Who will act as the advocate for the 'unwanted' children in a market-led allocation system where individual schools will determine which pupils they wish to admit? These are all important questions which arise from the implementation of these key pieces of legislation, but which are not addressed by them. The Education of Children in Need 283 CHILDREN IN NEED A second set of issues arises when we ask-who are the children in need within the education system? The Children Act in s.17 (10) gives a clear definition of children in need. A child shall be taken to be in need if: (a) he is unlikely to achieve or maintain, or to have the opportunity of achieving or maintaining, a reasonable standard of health or development without the provision for him of services by a local authority under this Part; (b) his health or development is likely to be significantly impaired, or further impaired, without the provision for him of such service; or (c) he is disabled. This definition is further elaborated in s. 17 (11) of the Children Act where it states that development means 'physical, intellectual, emotional, social or behavioural develop- ment'. It would seem clear from this definition that anyone who is not receiving appro- priate educational provision is 'a child in need'. Here it is possible to identify four key groups of young people who are children in need within the education system: children with special educational needs; children who are 'looked after' by the local authority; children who are excluded from school; and persistent non-attenders at school. These four groups are not mutually exclusive, indeed, as the research we shall discuss later shows, failure to provide services at one level often means that children become 'looked after' or are placed in special residential schools. There is already evidence that each of these groups is likely to be adversely affected by the contra- dictions in the Children Act and the Education Acts. Only brief mention of that evidence will be provided in this paper as these are issues addressed elsewhere in this volume. Children with Special Educational Needs Under the 1981 Education Act 'a child has "special educational needs" if he has a learning difficulty which calls for special educational provision to be made for him' and, it continues, a child has a 'learning difficulty' if he fulfills the following criteria: (a) he has a significantly greater difficulty in learning than the majority of children of his age; or (b) he has a disability which either prevents or hinders him from making use of educational facilities of a kind generally provided in schools, within the area of the local authority concerned, for children of his age. The Warnock Committee estimated that 20% of pupils would have a special educa- tional need (SEN) during their school life, but as the special need of some pupils is temporary, the proportion of pupils with a special need at any one time was approxi- mately 16%. Currently 2.1% of the total school population of England and Wales have a state- ment and the majority of these children attend special schools-although research suggests that recent rises in these numbers have resulted from the recent legislative changes (Lunt & Evans, 1991). A report by the Audit Commission and HMI has been highly critical of the statementing process and welcome changes have since been included in the Education Act 1993 (Audit Commission and HMI, 1992). However, the other 18% of children with special needs but without 'statements' have received relatively little attention in either research or policy arenas. The problems of these children will be diverse and will include physical disabilities, learning difficulties, specific reading, writing or language problems, behavioural or social problems. However, unlike 'statemented' children, children in this group have very few, if any, formal mechanisms which enable them to be considered for additional resources which are allocated to meet individual needs. Additional resources may come in two ways-through the use of centrally maintained services, such as educational psychologists, or through an additional factor within the LEA formula for delegated budgets. However the component within the formula to meet additional/ social needs shows widespread variation in both method of derivation and amount (Lee, 1991). Experience suggests that formula funding has the effect of transferring funds from disadvantaged schools as the positive discrimination of the LEA is no longer possible, and within schools, of resources going to more 'academic' interests (Howsden, 1993). Children excluded from school The number of pupils being excluded from school is increasing (see for instance NUT, 1992; Islington, 1992). Even the woefully inadequate National Exclusions Reporting System, established by DFE, paints a picture of many pupils excluded from school and with alternatives which are usually limited and fall far short of giving these pupils access to a full curriculum (Audit Commission and HMI, 1992; DFE, 1992). The conse- quences for these pupils in terms of their subsequent life chances are particularly worrying (Blyth & Milner, 1993). These concerns have prompted some significant and welcome changes in the new education law. Only time will tell whether these will be sufficient to counteract other influences. Research into the schooling of children with emotional or behavioural difficulties suggests some of the reasons for increased exclusions among this group (Stirling, 1991). First, that exclusion is being used increasingly to relieve schools of problem pupils, as it has the advantage of being speedy and almost autonomous in comparison to the process of 'statementing' under the 1981 Education Act. Second, the exclusion of difficult pupils is likely to match the priorities of the headteacher and board of governors, who are aware of the need for the school to 'score well' on published performance measures if it is to retain or enhance its budget. Another worrying aspect centres on racial harassment and the disproportionate number of black pupils who are excluded; for example in Birmingham, African- Caribbean children make up 9% of the total school population but 30% of the children who are excluded (Mayet, 1992; see also Nottinghamshire CC, 1989). Children looked after by the Local Authority The third group who, by definition, are children in need are those children being looked after by the local authority. Research studies have consistently reported the very low level of educational attainment of children who are in contact with social services or in care (Jackson, 1989; Aldgate, 1990; Garnett, 1992). Other studies point to the problems of the education provided to children whilst in care (Hampshire SSD, 1991; Fletcher-Campbell & Hall, 1990). This concern was pointedly raised again in the Utting Report, Children in the Public Care, which recommends that joint subcommittees of Education and Social Services should include, within their remit, the development of strategies to meet the educa- tional needs of children in care (Utting, 1991). Such a recommendation once again raises questions about the viability of such corporate strategies, given the very reduced power of the LEA to influence the policies and practices of individual schools to ensure that the educational needs of all 'children in need' are met. Persistent non-school attenders Pupils fail to attend school regularly for a variety of reasons. The HMI suggest that these include 'for example, family circumstances, cultural and social expectations and economic pressures; apathy or even antipathy to school on the part of pupils or parents or both and the fact that some pupils, for whatever reason, prefer other ways of spending their time... Attendance is also substantially affected by what schools do. The curriculum, the liveliness and competence of the teaching, the quality of the relation- ships and of the school as a community'. In this latter context two significant factors are bullying and racial harassment (HMI, 1989). Non-school attendance is not a new phenomenon, nor is there evidence that it has risen markedly in recent years (Gray & Jesson, 1990). Each school is now required to collect and publish information on 'unauthorised absences', but the widespread vari- ation in the interpretation of this requirement suggests that the first set of published figures must be treated with extreme caution (DFE, 1993b). However, there is other evidence that indicates the level of school attendance is very variable between schools and appears to be associated as much with school management as with socio-economic factors (Carlen et al., 1992; Grimshaw & Pratt, 1986; DES, 1989). Whether non-attendance is viewed as a rational choice (the consumer reject- ing the service offered) or the result of individual, community or school pathologies, the outcome is often that the child or young person comes to the attention of the social services department or the juvenile justice system. In this sense, and because they are not receiving appropriate services, non-school attenders are children in need. Adolescents assessed by Social Services We turn now to the second study which we are using to illustrate the importance of the concept of children in need within the education sector. The main purpose of this study was to examine the effectiveness of different forms of social work assessment with adolescents. Information was gathered on a group of 75 young people in one London borough, who were subject to assessment following one of three key events: consider- ation of care or accommodation, admission to care or accommodation, or a placement breakdown. Although the trigger events that called forth an assessment were related to social services provision, it was immediately clear from the assessment of these young people's needs that education was a hugely significant factor for young people. Indeed, both parents and social workers had identified 'persistent non-school attendance' as the main presenting problem for two-thirds of the sample who were of school age. Simply chronicling their educational status at the time of their assessment makes it abundantly clear why this should be the case. First of all, it is necessary to give some brief information about the sample of 75 young people. The focus of the study was on adolescents, so the modal age of the group was 15, with two-thirds of the sample aged between 14 and 16 years. A similar proportion (63%) were from minority ethnic groups, and from a very varied range of ethnic origins. Boys made up more than half of the group (55%) and tended to be younger than the girls. The vast majority (81%) were under school leaving age. Of these, their official educational status was that just over half (51%) were enrolled in mainstream schools; 13% were in special schools (day or boarding); 16% were receiving part-time education at home or in a special tuition unit (although hours were very varied and none more than half the time); 20% were not enrolled in any school or alternative provision. In addition, 28% of the group were subject to a statement of SEN or were going through the statementing process. Not only were one in five of this group not currently being provided with education, but for many this situation had prevailed for long periods of time. Indeed, in this sample one in four of all the school children had been out of school for more than one year at the time of their assessment. How could so many children fall through the education net? Three factors were at play. First, pupils waiting for a statement of SEN may not be offered any immediate alternative. This study included one young man who had been waiting two years for a statement of SEN and during that time he had not been provided with any form of education. Second, a high proportion of pupils permanently excluded from school had not been provided with any other form of educational support. Sixteen per cent of the research group had been excluded, three-quarters of them permanently. Third, even for those officially in school, many were very poor attenders. For both this group and those excluded this problem was often worse in their last year of school. In this situation social workers certainly believed that the edu- cation department was deliberately slow in responding to these young people's needs, or gave them such a low priority that they fell out of the system before being dealt with. The results of such a policy can be seen among the older school leavers in the sample group-fewer than a quarter had actually attended school up to their official leaving date-and none of them had any GCSEs or any other educational qualifications. This brief account of the educational background of this group of adolescents raises several issues: * the majority of these young people were not in care or being 'looked after' by the local authority, when this data was gathered. This highlights just why it is so crucially important to think about the education of children in need and not just about those within the care system; * the failure to identify or to deal adequately with school problems at an early stage increases the chances of these young people coming to the attention of the care or juvenile justice systems; * even when young people do become known to social services, the slowness of the educational assessment process can often lead to what may be called 'planning blight' in the social services. This is particularly so if there is a possibility that the education department will recommend a place in a special boarding school, which may have a major impact on social services care plans for the young person; * alternative education provision currently fails to meet the demand and in many cases is not of sufficient quality, as the government has acknowledged (Ofsted, 1993; DFE, 1993); * there is evidence of growing tension between professionals in education and SSDs, often despite feelings of goodwill and shared aims, but the ability to work together effectively is being hampered by arguments over budgets and the growing practice of having to contract or buy in services once freely exchanged. The irrefutable evidence of these two studies is of children in need within the education system: children who do not have 'the opportunity of achieving or maintaining a reasonably standard of development, or whose development is likely to be significantly impaired', because of a lack of services. All the evidence so far of the impact of the Education Reform Act 1988, now to be compounded by the Education Act 1993-in- creases in the numbers statemented and in children excluded from school, of new admissions policies, of the transfer of resources away from support services-makes it more urgent that an answer is found to the question: How are we to ensure that these children in need receive the range and level of services appropriate to their needs, as statutorily required by the Children Act 1989?
